name: Carlos Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a city crew for the power company, mostly underground cable and the green boxes on street corners, plus a lot of new connections for flats and car chargers. Morning starts at the Harbour Road depot, then we're in a hole in the pavement with buses going past, jointing an eleven-thousand-volt cable by hand. I love jointing, it's like surgery with gloves on. What wears me out is the traffic permits and the people shouting at us for blocking their parking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, who's around you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nobody at home but me and a very fat cat called Bolt. I rent a studio near the canal, I've got about five months of savings, and I spend too much on gadgets. I use AI every day, honestly, I ask it about fault readings, I get it to quiz me for my next exam, I even had it plan my mum's birthday dinner. My mum still thinks I should have been an engineer, so I'm doing an online course in grid automation at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? That would actually disappoint me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but still useful, because for me it is. I'd show the crew how I use it to check cable ratings in ten seconds. Online I'd probably post a slightly grumpy thread about how the hype distracted from the real need, which is more people on the grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing bad happens. The city keeps adding chargers and heat pumps, so there's more work than crews, and my job's as safe as it gets. If AI turns out to be a fancy calculator, I'm still the guy in the hole on Harbour Road with the busiest cable diary in the city. I'd just feel I'd bet a bit too hard on the future being exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the crew and finish the grid automation course anyway, because the grid is getting smarter even without big AI. Keep putting about four hundred a month into savings. Maybe take the senior jointer exam next autumn, since that's a pay bump either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. I like change, so a world where nothing changes sounds a bit grey, but it's not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel you bet too hard on the future. What did you bet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Evenings, mostly. Two years of nights on that course instead of football. I'd still finish it, though, because the company's putting sensors into every substation regardless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you in this picture at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent. My landlord's put it up twice in two years. On my pay it's fine, but it means I'm not buying anywhere in this city before I'm forty unless something changes.

say: I'd call AI **overhyped but useful**, and show the crew my cable checks.
I'd post that the real need is **more people** on the grid.
think: My job stays **very safe** because chargers and heat pumps keep coming.
I'd feel I **bet too hard** on an exciting future.
do: Sit the **senior jointer exam** next autumn for a pay rise.
feel: **Calm** but a bit flat, since he enjoys change.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be a fancy calculator, I'm still the guy in the hole on Harbour Road with the busiest cable diary in the city.
fieldNote: He is a **daily AI user** who would miss the excitement more than fear the change.
City demand for **chargers and heat pumps** keeps his work secure.
His only pressure is **rising rent**, which pushes buying past forty.

steps.text: Finish the online grid automation course at night
Save about four hundred a month toward a deposit
Sit the senior jointer exam next autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I'd bet on, honestly. It's already happening at our depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our chance, the grid needs a hundred new skills and we should grab them. I'd push the union to get the company to pay for AI and automation training for everyone, not just the young ones. Online I'd write about how public money should cushion the people in the office who get hit first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good. The permits and the job scheduling, the bit I hate, go to software. I keep the jointing, which is hands-on, and I've got the automation course, so I'm ahead. The people I'd worry about are the planners, and my mum, who does accounts at a bus company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be the depot's test user for the new scheduling system in the first month. I'd finish the automation course and apply for the smart grid technician role in the control centre within the year. I'd also sit down with my mum and help her learn the accounting tools so she isn't the one left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually excited. It's the first picture where I feel like the future is lined up for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help your mum. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. She'd say she's fifty-eight and doesn't need a computer telling her how to do sums. I'd sit with my mum every Sunday at her kitchen table until the accounts software felt like hers, not something done to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hamid, the planner who builds our job packs. He's brilliant at it, but it's exactly what software will do. I'd try to get him onto the automation course with me so he has somewhere to go.

say: I'd call it **our chance**, with the grid needing new skills.
I'd ask for **public money** to cushion office workers hit first.
think: Losing **permits and scheduling** to software suits me fine.
I worry about **planners** and my mum, who does accounts.
do: Volunteer as the depot's **test user** for new scheduling software.
Apply for the **smart grid technician** role within the year.
Help his mum learn **accounting software** on Sundays.
feel: **Calm** and excited, as if the future is lined up for him.
S1.quote: I'd sit with my mum every Sunday at her kitchen table until the accounts software felt like hers, not something done to her.
fieldNote: He reads the change as **good for him**, because he has prepared and his work is hands-on.
His concern turns outward to **his mum and Hamid**, both thinking workers.
He wants **public support** for those hit first, matching his progressive views.

steps.text: Volunteer as test user for the depot's new scheduling software
Apply for a smart grid technician job in the control centre
Teach his mum the accounting software on Sunday visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for AI, five for robots. That flips my control-centre plan on its head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this needs a government response on the scale of a war, with income support and retraining at once. At the depot I'd tell people not to panic but to get on every new kit trial. Online I'd be loud, honestly, I'd be posting every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The control centre job I wanted is thinking work, so it's gone by 2028. The jointing lasts until about 2031. So my safest bet becomes the people who fix and run the robots, which is hands-on plus tech, and I'd be good at it. But I'd be one of a thousand linemen chasing the same roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the control-centre plan and switch to a robotics maintenance certificate straight away, evenings and weekends. I'd push my savings from five months to eight by cutting the gadget habit and moving to a cheaper flat further out. I'd get on the union's tech committee so workers have a say on which robots go near live cables.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not wrecked, because I'd have a plan, but I'd know the plan could fail. I spent two years training for the control room, and in this picture the control room is the first thing to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving further out is a big step. Would you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, within six months. The studio is nice but it's a third of my pay. If my job's got a three-year clock on it, I'd rather have a longer bus ride and a fatter savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she should probably take early retirement if they offer it, because her accounting work goes in 2028. And that I'd help with money if it came to that, which is a weird thing to say to your mum at twenty-seven.

say: I'd call for a **war-scale response** with income support and retraining.
I'd urge the depot to join **every kit trial** rather than panic.
think: The **control-centre job** I wanted goes by 2028 because it's thinking work.
Robot maintenance is my best bet, but **a thousand linemen** will chase it.
do: Switch to a **robotics maintenance** certificate on evenings and weekends.
Move to a **cheaper flat** within six months to reach eight months saved.
Join the union's **tech committee** on robots near live cables.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan he knows might fail.
S2.quote: I spent two years training for the control room, and in this picture the control room is the first thing to go.
fieldNote: The fast timeline breaks his **two-year plan**, because the control room is thinking work.
He moves quickly: **new course, cheaper flat** and union role within months.
He feels he may need to **support his mum**, a role reversal.

steps.text: Switch study to a robotics maintenance certificate on weekends
Move to a cheaper flat further from the canal within six months
Sit on the union tech committee for robots near live cables
Cut gadget spending and push savings to eight months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031 and 2034. I'd be thirty-five when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this right, and I'd keep pushing for a public training fund. To the crew I'd say pick your next skill now and the company should pay. I'd post a lot less in this one, because there's work to do instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd still get a few years out of the automation course before the control room changes. Then I'd move into robot maintenance around 2031, ahead of the rush. Honestly, I think I come out fine, maybe better paid. A five-year warning is long enough for someone like me to be the person who fixes the robots instead of the person they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the automation course by next summer, then start the robotics certificate in 2028. I'd stay in the studio but stop buying gadgets and put the difference into a pension. I'd also lean on the union to make sure the older guys get the same training slots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, and I'd worry about friends, but I'd feel ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the older guys should get the same slots. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I learned jointing from Frank, who's fifty-six. He taught me for free, basically. If the company only trains young people, that's a betrayal of the guys who built the crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where it goes wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robot makers keep the repair work to themselves, like phone companies do. Then there's no robot maintenance job for me. That's why I'd want rules on the right to repair, written now.

say: I'd say there is **time** to do this right with a public training fund.
I'd tell the crew to **pick a next skill** on company time.
think: I'd move into **robot maintenance** around 2031, ahead of the rush.
I could come out **better paid**, which surprises me.
do: Finish the **automation course** by next summer and start robotics in 2028.
Stop buying gadgets and put the difference into a **pension**.
Push the union for **equal training slots** for older linemen.
feel: **Uneasy**, worried for friends but feeling ahead of the change.
S3.quote: A five-year warning is long enough for someone like me to be the person who fixes the robots instead of the person they replace.
fieldNote: Five years lets him be **early** rather than chasing roles.
He owes **Frank, his mentor**, and wants older workers trained too.
He spots a hidden risk in **right to repair** for robot makers.

steps.text: Start a robotics maintenance certificate in 2028
Redirect gadget money into a pension each month
Lobby for right-to-repair rules on grid robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 and 2039. That's my whole thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best version, a decade to build the training and the rules. I'd still post, but more like 'here's what I'm learning' than shouting. To the crew I'd say enjoy the jointing and keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd do the control room job for six or seven years and then move to robot fleet work. I'd probably earn more and climb into holes less. Ten years is a whole career change for me, and my knees would thank the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the automation course, get the control-centre job within two years, and start saving properly for a flat. I'd join the union's tech committee anyway. Around 2033 I'd start the robotics side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly. It feels like a career ladder rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hole on Harbour Road, oddly. Buses going past, the smell of the cable compound, the crew passing tea down. You can't get that in a control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at buying a small flat outside the city in about five years. Bolt would get a garden, which he doesn't deserve.

say: I'd call it the **best version**, with a decade to build training and rules.
I'd post about **what I'm learning** instead of shouting.
think: I'd do the **control room** for years, then move to robot fleet work.
I'd likely **earn more** and spend less time in holes.
do: Land the **control-centre job** within two years.
Save toward a **small flat** outside the city in about five years.
feel: **Calm** and excited, as if it's a career ladder, not a cliff.
S4.quote: Ten years is a whole career change for me, and my knees would thank the robots.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him live his **original plan** and then move again.
He shows **nostalgia** for jointing even as he looks forward.
An adaptive, single worker with savings stays **calm** at the far end.

steps.text: Apply for a control-centre job within two years
Save for a small flat outside the city

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, mostly because the job I've been training for disappears before I can even use it. What would help is a public training fund that pays for robotics courses for linemen, and a law that lets independent technicians repair grid robots. My cable knowledge is only worth something if the robot makers are forced to let us open the box.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the savings. If the power company saves millions on crews, I'd want some of that back on people's bills or into the training fund. Otherwise it's just my job turned into someone else's bonus.

headlineQuote: My cable knowledge is only worth something if the robot makers are forced to let us open the box.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old city crew lead** who joints underground cable and uses AI tools every day.
He lives alone with **a cat called Bolt**, rents a studio and studies grid automation at night.
He sees **Steady Disruption** as good for him and worries more for his mum and the planners.
AGI by 2028 breaks his **control-room plan**, so he pivots fast to robot maintenance.
His politics show in calls for **public training funds** and right-to-repair rules.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the control-room job he's training for disappears first.
whatWouldHelp: A **public training fund** for linemen and **right-to-repair** rules for grid robots.
